strengths: Clear research gap identification: the paper convincingly positions Rank-Learner as the first model-agnostic, Neyman-orthogonal two-stage learner for directly ranking treatment effects (Table 1), distinct from CATE estimators (DR-/R-learners) and non-orthogonal rankers (Kamran et al. 2024; Vanderschueren et al. 2024).

The theory is carefully developed: the influence-function derivation of the orthogonal pairwise loss (Appendix C) is complete and self-contained, the Neyman-orthogonality proof (Theorem 5.1) explicitly verifies the cross-derivative condition for each nuisance component, and Theorem 5.2 verifies that the orthogonal loss retains the correct population minimizers. The pseudo-label interpretation (uncertainty-weighted DR-score correction) is intuitive and well explained.

Excellent experimental design for isolating the two claimed benefits: baselines are chosen so that (i) direct ranking vs. full CATE estimation and (ii) orthogonal vs. plug-in objectives can be disentangled; the plug-in ranker fairly represents the strategy of Vanderschueren et al. (2024), and the tree ranker of Kamran et al. (2024) is included as an additional comparison in Appendix F with matched nuisance estimates and tuning protocol.

Useful ablations: pair subsampling shows ~1% of n² pairs suffices (making the method practical), overlap sensitivity confirms robustness across the full overlap range, and nuisance-estimation quality (Table 6) connects empirical gaps to the theory (larger gains in small-sample regimes with larger nuisance error).

Clear presentation with a well-structured motivation section explaining why the binary ranking loss is non-differentiable in τ and why the smooth surrogate enables orthogonalization; the κ parameter analysis (Appendix D.2) is thorough and honest about the bias-variance trade-off.
weaknesses: Empirical improvements are modest and statistical significance is never assessed. At n=500–2,000 and on semi-synthetic benchmarks, gains over the DR-learner are small (e.g., 1.30 vs 1.28, 1.35 vs 1.34, 1.18 vs 1.16) relative to reported standard deviations over only five seeds; no paired significance tests or confidence intervals on differences are provided. The headline claim of 'consistently outperforms' rests on small mean differences.

The claim that ranking is an 'easier' problem than CATE estimation is supported only at the informal population level (larger minimizer class for L^bin). No statistical learning theory quantifies this advantage (e.g., convergence rates for the ranking loss vs. the CATE loss under the cited Foster & Syrgkanis framework); orthogonality is proven, but the fast-rate implications for the pairwise loss are not established.

Evaluation is entirely synthetic/semi-synthetic with treatment effects constructed as strictly increasing transformations of a latent score, i.e., DGPs tailored to the ranking task's structure; no real-world dataset with actual treatment assignment (e.g., RCT or uplift benchmarks) is included, so practical benefit in realistic settings remains unverified.

The pseudo labels can fall outside (0,1) and are clipped as a stabilization; this ad hoc fix is disclosed but unanalyzed, and its interaction with orthogonality and the κ-selection procedure is not discussed.

Comparison to Vanderschueren et al. (2024) is only indirect (via the plug-in ranker); while the argument is plausible, direct replication of at least one of their configurations would strengthen the empirical positioning.

Only feedforward networks with a single hidden layer are used for all methods; robustness of the conclusions to other model classes (e.g., gradient boosting, causal forests for nuisances) is untested despite the model-agnostic claim.

strengths: The research gap is clearly identified and well-motivated: existing methods either estimate CATE magnitudes or learn treatment-effect rankings with non-orthogonal objectives (Table 1), and the paper positions Rank-Learner as the first model-agnostic, Neyman-orthogonal two-stage learner for ranking treatment effects.

The technical development is careful and transparent: the smooth surrogate targets (Eq. 9-10) are a sensible way to make the ranking objective differentiable in the nuisances, the influence-function derivation in Appendix C is step-by-step, and the Neyman-orthogonality proof (Theorem 5.1) checks each nuisance component explicitly, including the subtlety that the pseudo labels can leave the (0,1) range.

The experimental design is commendably structured to isolate the two claimed benefits: comparing against T-learner/DR-learner (direct ranking vs. pointwise CATE) and against a plug-in ranker with identical architecture and targets but no orthogonal correction (orthogonal vs. plug-in). Additional ablations on pair subsampling, overlap sensitivity, and nuisance estimation quality (Tables 5-6) support the mechanistic story.

Writing and presentation are generally clear, with good figures (Figure 1, 2), a useful summary of learning objectives (Table 2), and honest discussion of the kappa bias-variance trade-off and the pseudo-label clipping heuristic.
weaknesses: The central narrative is in tension with the paper's own theory. The paper claims CATE estimation 'solves a harder problem than necessary,' but Theorem 5.2 shows the orthogonal loss is minimized by g(x) = tau(x)/kappa + c — i.e., it still requires recovering the (scaled) CATE function, not merely its ordering. Only the binary loss L^bin targets pure ranking, and it cannot be orthogonalized. Thus the method is best understood as a rescaled, corrected CATE learner, and the claimed advantage over the DR-learner (which also recovers tau orthogonally) is conceptually under-explained.

Empirical gains are modest and lack statistical support. Improvements over the DR-learner and plug-in ranker are frequently within one standard deviation (e.g., 1.30 vs 1.28 at n=500; 1.35 vs 1.34 on MovieLens; 1.18 vs 1.16 on MIMIC-III), no significance tests are reported, and at n=100 Rank-Learner is actually outperformed by the tree ranker in Table 7. 'Consistently outperforms' is therefore an overstatement of small, noisy differences.

There is a potential model-selection asymmetry that could favor the proposed method: ranking methods are tuned via approximated validation AUTOC while CATE estimators use their standard validation loss, yet the final evaluation metric is exactly AUTOC. This confound is not discussed or ablated.

Theoretical guarantees are thinner than the abstract suggests. 'Strong theoretical guarantees' amounts to first-order orthogonality plus correct population minimizers; no excess-risk or convergence-rate results are provided (the cited Foster & Syrgkanis machinery is invoked but not used), and the clipping of pseudo labels to (0,1) in practice breaks the conditions under which orthogonality is established.

The baseline set is narrow: only T-learner, DR-learner, a plug-in ranker, and (appendix-only) one tree ranker. The R-learner, causal forests, and other established estimators are absent, and all models are single-hidden-layer neural networks, raising questions about generalization of the conclusions.

The semi-synthetic benchmarks still use fully simulated treatments, outcomes, and effects; only covariates are real. Given the small margins and the synthetic nature of all evaluations, evidence of practical usefulness on genuinely realistic problems remains limited.

strengths: The paper identifies a genuine and well-motivated gap: no existing method for ranking individuals by treatment effects is both model-agnostic and Neyman-orthogonal (Table 1 positioning is clear and fair to prior work such as Kamran et al. 2024 and Vanderschueren et al. 2024).

The core theory is sound and complete. The derivation of the efficient influence function of the soft pairwise loss (Appendix C) is careful, and the proof of Neyman-orthogonality (Theorem 5.1) explicitly verifies the cross-derivative condition for each nuisance component. Theorem 5.2 correctly characterizes the population minimizers, and Appendix D gives an insightful analysis of the role of the smoothness parameter kappa, including the honest observation that for finite kappa the loss actually identifies a scaled CATE.

The implementation is elegant: because binary cross-entropy is affine in the label, the entire one-step correction is absorbed into the pseudo labels, so the second stage reduces to standard pairwise ranking with corrected targets. This makes the method easy to adopt and model-agnostic as claimed.

Experiments are well designed to disentangle the two claimed benefits (direct ranking vs. CATE estimation; orthogonal vs. plug-in objectives), with useful ablations on pair subsampling, overlap sensitivity, sample-size scaling, and nuisance estimation quality (Table 6), plus a comparison to the tree ranker of Kamran et al. (2024) with matched nuisance estimates and tuning protocol.
The paper is clearly written, with good intuition sections (e.g., the pseudo-label and kappa discussions), reproducible details (Appendix E), and code availability.
weaknesses: The central 'easier problem' motivation is partially undercut by the paper's own theory: for any fixed finite kappa, Theorem 5.2 shows the orthogonal loss is minimized by g(x) = tau(x)/kappa + c, i.e., a full (scaled) CATE function is still being recovered, not just an ordering. The distinction between the CATE loss and the ranking loss is thus weaker in practice than the introduction suggests, and the empirical story mostly reduces to 'orthogonalization helps,' which is already known from the DR-learner.

Empirical gains over the strongest baselines are small and sometimes within noise. On the semi-synthetic benchmarks the AUTOC differences are e.g. 1.35 vs. 1.34 (MovieLens) and 1.18 vs. 1.16 (MIMIC-III) with overlapping standard deviations over only five seeds, and no statistical significance tests are reported. Similarly, the plug-in ranker underperforms the DR-learner on MovieLens, which weakens the claim that direct ranking is systematically easier than CATE estimation; the narrative that both factors contribute is only partially supported.

All evaluation is on synthetic and semi-synthetic data with author-designed data-generating processes in which the ground-truth ranking is by construction a monotone transform of a latent score. No real-data experiment (e.g., with policy-value estimation on an RCT or observational study) is provided, so it remains unclear how the method behaves when the identification assumptions or the DGP design choices do not hold.

Model selection for the rankers uses an approximated AUTOC (Chernozhukov et al., 2025) on the validation set, which itself depends on nuisance estimates, introducing a potential circularity that could favor the ranking methods relative to CATE estimators selected by their standard validation loss. This fairness concern is not discussed.

The pseudo labels are clipped to (0,1) as a stabilization step (Appendix E.3), which silently breaks the exact orthogonality property proven in Theorem 5.1 in those cases; the practical impact is unquantified.

The theoretical contribution, while correct, is largely an application of the standard one-step/influence-function orthogonalization recipe (Kennedy, 2024; Foster & Syrgkanis, 2023) to an existing soft ranking loss (already used by Vanderschueren et al., 2024). No convergence-rate results or finite-sample guarantees specific to the ranking objective are provided, which limits the depth of the theoretical contribution beyond the orthogonality check.

A limitations section is absent from the main paper; constraints such as the binary treatment and continuous outcome setting, the dependence on unconfoundedness, and the kappa selection issue are only touched on indirectly.

strengths: Clear identification of a genuine research gap: the paper convincingly argues (Table 1, related work) that existing methods either estimate CATE magnitudes or use non-orthogonal ranking objectives, and positions Rank-Learner as the first model-agnostic two-stage learner that is both direct (ranking) and Neyman-orthogonal.

Careful and complete theory: the efficient influence function of the pairwise loss is derived from first principles (Appendix C), Neyman-orthogonality is proven rigorously for all three nuisance components, and the population optima of all four objectives are characterized (Theorem 5.2, Appendix D), including a thoughtful analysis of the smoothing parameter kappa and its bias-variance trade-off.

Extensive and well-designed experiments: fully synthetic benchmark with varying n and overlap, three semi-synthetic benchmarks with realistic covariates, the real-world CRITEO uplift benchmark, plus additional ACIC/IHDP evaluations, sensitivity analyses (kappa, nuisance misspecification, pseudo-label clipping, pair subsampling), and additional strong baselines (FlexTENet, PairNet, tree ranker) in the appendix.

Fair comparison methodology: identical architectures and training budgets across methods, with ablations that cleanly disentangle the effect of (i) direct ranking vs. CATE estimation and (ii) orthogonal vs. plug-in objectives; the plug-in ranker is a well-chosen ablation baseline.
Good presentation quality, honest discussion of practical issues (pseudo-label clipping, computational cost of pairwise training, role of kappa), and available code.
weaknesses: The core methodological contribution is fairly incremental: it applies the standard one-step/influence-function orthogonalization recipe (Kennedy 2024; Foster & Syrkanis 2023) to a pairwise soft ranking loss. The novelty lies in the combination and the derivation, not in a new learning principle.

There is a conceptual tension between the motivation and the theory: the paper motivates ranking as an 'easier' problem that avoids recovering CATE magnitudes, yet the population minimizer of the orthogonal loss is g = tau/kappa + c (Theorem 5.2), i.e., a scaled CATE. The orthogonality is achieved precisely because the smooth surrogate reintroduces dependence on effect magnitudes, so the practical benefit of 'not solving the harder problem' is weaker than claimed. The kappa analysis acknowledges this, but the framing in the abstract/introduction oversells it.

Empirical gains are modest and often within one standard deviation: e.g., on semi-synthetic benchmarks Rank-Learner's improvements over DR-learner and plug-in ranker are small (1.35 vs 1.34 on MovieLens; 1.18 vs 1.17 on MIMIC-III), and on the synthetic benchmark at n=2000 methods converge. No statistical significance tests are reported for the main comparisons; only 5 seeds are used.

The binary ranking loss L_bin (the most direct formalization of 'pure ranking') is not orthogonal, and the paper does not fully resolve why orthogonalizing the softer surrogate is the right design rather than, e.g., an orthogonal version based on a different ranking objective; the choice is justified post hoc via the influence function derivability.

Evaluation of AUTOC relies on an approximation of Chernozhukov et al. (2025) for unobserved treatment effects in semi-synthetic settings, and the real-world CRITEO experiment induces confounding synthetically, so the strongest claims about observational settings rest partly on simulated confounding.
Some references are unusual (e.g., ICML 2026 and 2026 journal citations), and the paper lacks a dedicated limitations section beyond the impact statement.

strengths: The problem of directly learning treatment effect rankings from observational data is well motivated, and the positioning relative to CATE estimation, uplift modeling, and prior ranking work (Kamran et al., 2024; Vanderschueren et al., 2024) is clearly laid out in Table 1.

The derivation of the influence function of the pairwise soft ranking loss and the one-step correction (Appendix C) is careful and complete, and the proof of Neyman-orthogonality (Theorem 5.1) is verified explicitly for each nuisance component.

The paper is honest about several of its own subtleties: it acknowledges that the population minimizers of the orthogonal loss recover a scaled CATE rather than only a ranking (Theorem 5.2, Table 2), that pseudo labels must be clipped in practice, and it studies clipping, κ sensitivity, overlap, and nuisance misspecification in the appendix.

The experimental protocol is broad (synthetic, three semi-synthetic benchmarks, CRITEO, plus ACIC/IHDP and additional baselines such as tree ranker, DR ranker, PairNet, and FlexTENet), and the plug-in ranker ablation usefully isolates the effect of orthogonalization.
The method is model-agnostic and computationally lightweight, with the pair-subsampling analysis showing the quadratic pairwise cost is manageable in practice.
weaknesses: The empirical evidence for the central claim is marginal and mostly within noise. On the synthetic benchmark at n = 1,000 Rank-Learner achieves 1.34 ± 0.01 vs. 1.33 ± 0.02 for the DR-learner, and on the semi-synthetic benchmarks the gaps over the DR-learner are 0.01–0.03, i.e., comparable to or smaller than the reported standard deviations. No statistical significance tests are reported anywhere. The CRITEO results have very large variances (e.g., 5.19 ± 1.87 vs. 4.44 ± 1.12 at 50k), so the headline real-world improvement is not statistically convincing.

There is an unresolved conceptual tension at the heart of the paper. The introduction and abstract argue that ranking is an easier problem than CATE estimation and that the proposed method avoids recovering effect magnitudes, yet Theorem 5.2 shows the actually-implementable loss identifies a scaled version of the full CATE, g(x) = τ(x)/κ + c. The purely-ranking objective (L^bin) is precisely the one that cannot be orthogonalized. Thus the practical contribution reduces to an influence-function-corrected plug-in soft ranking loss, and the 'easier problem' narrative is only realized in the κ → 0 limit, where the (1/κ)-scaled correction amplifies label noise — a bias-variance trade-off that is ultimately resolved by tuning on an approximate AUTOC criterion.

The theory is a fairly direct application of existing machinery (one-step correction and influence functions following Kennedy 2024, Foster & Syrgkanis 2023, and the proof strategy of Morzywolek et al. 2024). No convergence rates or oracle inequalities are derived despite orthogonality typically implying them; the theoretical novelty is an adaptation rather than a new result.

A theory-to-practice gap: the implemented objective clips pseudo labels to (0,1), which means the loss actually optimized is not the one proven orthogonal. The gradient-sensitivity diagnostic (Fig. 7) mitigates this somewhat but does not restore the formal guarantee, and clipping itself depends on nuisance estimates.

The synthetic and semi-synthetic design may favor the proposed method: treatment effects are generated as a strictly increasing transform of a latent score s(x), and treatment assignment and outcomes also depend on s(x), so the ground-truth ranking is a relatively smooth, low-complexity function of covariates that outcome prediction can partially recover. Sample sizes are small (n ≤ 2,000) and all models are tiny single-hidden-layer networks, leaving the behavior under realistic scales and stronger nuisance learners unexamined.

On the additional ACIC/IHDP benchmarks (Table 13), results are mixed: Rank-Learner has an overall win rate of only 40% on IHDP (losing to the DR-learner's 42%), and the selection of only 'replications with substantial heterogeneity' for ACIC introduces a post-hoc filtering choice that is not fully justified.

Reproducibility of the semi-synthetic experiments depends on data-generating processes specified only in a code repository rather than in the paper, and the code URL is incomplete in the manuscript; the ACIC replication filtering and the κ/model-selection procedure involve undocumented researcher degrees of freedom.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: directly learning rankings of treatment effects from observational data, with a convincing argument that standard CATE estimation solves a harder problem than necessary for ranking.

Novel and technically clean contribution: the first Neyman-orthogonal two-stage learner for treatment-effect ranking. The smooth pairwise surrogate (L^soft) is a sensible bridge that makes influence-function-based orthogonalization possible, and the resulting pseudo-label construction (Eq. 12) has an intuitive interpretation (correction weight concentrated on ambiguous pairs).

Complete theoretical treatment: the derivation of the efficient influence function of the pairwise loss (Appendix C.1), the one-step correction, and the cross-derivative orthogonality proof (Appendix C.4) are careful and appear correct; Theorem 5.2 verifies the population minimizers still preserve the treatment-effect ordering, addressing the key concern that orthogonalization might distort the target.

Well-designed experiments that disentangle the two claimed benefits: direct ranking vs. CATE estimation (T-/DR-learner baselines) and orthogonal vs. plug-in objectives (plug-in ranker baseline). Results consistently support both claims, with the largest gains in small-sample regimes where nuisance error dominates, matching theory.

Extensive robustness analyses: overlap sensitivity, nuisance misspecification, pseudo-label clipping, kappa sensitivity, pair subsampling, and additional baselines (tree ranker, DR ranker, PairNet, FlexTENet) plus ACIC/IHDP benchmarks, all with reasonable protocols and honest reporting (e.g., FlexTENet slightly better at n=2,000 in Table 12).
Good reproducibility: detailed DGP specifications, implementation details, and a stated code release.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is somewhat incremental: the contribution is essentially a one-step influence-function correction applied to a smooth pairwise BCE loss using standard DR pseudo-outcomes; an expert reader could anticipate this construction, and the proofs follow well-trodden templates (Kennedy 2024; Morzywolek et al. 2024).

There is a tension between the core motivation and the theory: the paper argues CATE estimation is 'harder than necessary,' yet Theorem 5.2 shows the orthogonal loss's population minimizer is a scaled CATE, (1/kappa)*tau(x)+c. The 'pure ranking' regime arises only as kappa->0, which conflicts with the need for finite kappa to make the loss differentiable and orthogonalizable; the bias-variance discussion mitigates but does not fully resolve this, and the framing slightly oversells the 'easier problem' story.

Pseudo labels are clipped to (0,1), which strictly speaking breaks the proven Neyman-orthogonality of the implemented objective; the paper addresses this only empirically (gradient-sensitivity diagnostic), and no formal guarantees apply to the clipped variant.

Model selection (kappa and other hyperparameters) relies on the approximated AUTOC criterion of Chernozhukov et al. (2025), which introduces an additional estimation layer whose own error properties are not analyzed; it is unclear how sensitive the comparisons are to this choice.

Empirical gains over the plug-in ranker and DR-learner are modest at larger sample sizes (e.g., 1.34 vs. 1.33 AUTOC at n=1,000; near-ties in Table 12 and Table 13 win rates), so the practical advantage is concentrated in small-n / high-nuisance-error regimes; the CRITEO results have large standard deviations relative to the improvements.

All experiments use simple single-hidden-layer networks and small n (<= 2,000 train; 10k CRITEO train), so scalability claims of the model-agnostic design are not stressed; no statistical significance tests are reported for the headline comparisons.

The main-table implementation and the CATENets-style implementation (Table 12) yield noticeably different absolute results for the same method, which is disclosed but slightly muddies the empirical picture.
